title: SEBI Eases KYC Rules for NRIs as India Pushes to Attract Diaspora Investment
excerpt: India's securities regulator has removed the requirement for NRIs to be physically present in India for digital KYC verification, while industry bodies push for further reforms to make investing from abroad seamless.
body:
• SEBI has removed the requirement for existing NRI clients to be physically present in India during digital re-KYC verification
  • The Startup Policy Forum has submitted recommendations to SEBI and the finance ministry to extend digital KYC to new NRI account openings as well
  • The RBI has proposed doubling the NRI/OCI individual shareholding limit in listed Indian companies from 5% to 10% under the Portfolio Investment Scheme
  • Industry groups want SEBI and IFSCA KYC systems made interoperable so NRIs do not have to repeat verification across frameworks

India's securities regulator has taken its clearest step yet toward making it easier for Non-Resident Indians and Overseas Citizens of India to invest in Indian markets without flying back to complete paperwork. SEBI removed the requirement for existing NRI clients to be physically located in India during digital re-KYC verification — and a growing industry push aims to extend that relief to new account openings as well.

What Changed: Re-KYC Without Being in India

In a circular issued in December 2025, SEBI modified its digital onboarding provisions to allow existing NRI clients to complete their re-KYC process from abroad. Previously, SEBI's KYC Master Circular required the digital verification app to confirm that the client was physically located within India — a requirement that forced NRIs to either visit India or fall back on a cumbersome offline process of couriering notarized documents.

Under the revised rules, the digital KYC app must still employ safeguards including random action prompts, time-stamped interactions, and geo-tagging. The GPS coordinates captured by the app must match the country listed in the client's address proof, and the app must block any connections from spoofed IP addresses. But the critical change is that the location no longer needs to be India — it just needs to match the client's documented overseas address.

"Our members, including some of India's largest investment platforms, are telling us this friction is real, and it's costing India inflows it doesn't need to lose."

— Shweta Raj Kohli, President and CEO, Startup Policy Forum

The Push for Full Digital Onboarding

While the re-KYC relaxation helps existing NRI investors maintain their accounts, opening a new securities account still requires physical presence in India for digital onboarding. This gap has become a focal point for industry advocacy.

The Startup Policy Forum (SPF), an alliance representing India's new-age companies, submitted a note to SEBI and the finance ministry highlighting the operational challenges NRIs face. Among its key recommendations: scrapping the India-only geo-tagging requirement for NRI video KYC on new accounts, allowing uploaded wet signatures to be verified during video calls instead of requiring Aadhaar-based e-sign, and making the KYC systems of SEBI and the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) interoperable.

The Aadhaar issue is particularly acute. While multiple forms of digital signatures are technically permitted, most financial intermediaries rely on Aadhaar-based e-Sign because it is the most widely integrated option. Many NRIs either do not have Aadhaar or face challenges receiving OTPs linked to it while abroad, which effectively forces the process to go physical.

RBI Also Opens the Door Wider

The regulatory momentum extends beyond SEBI. The Reserve Bank of India has proposed doubling the individual shareholding limit for NRIs and OCIs in listed Indian companies from 5% to 10% under the Portfolio Investment Scheme, without requiring registration as foreign portfolio investors. The move, if finalized, would give diaspora investors significantly greater room to build positions in Indian equities.

However, industry executives argue that raising investment limits alone will not attract greater NRI participation unless the onboarding friction is also resolved. Foreign portfolio investors sold Indian equities worth nearly Rs 2.25 trillion in 2026, exceeding the total outflow of Rs 1.66 trillion in 2025 — underscoring the need for alternative pools of patient capital.

What It Means for NRIs

For NRIs already invested in Indian markets, the re-KYC relaxation means they no longer need to plan a trip to India just to keep their accounts active. Periodic KYC updates can now be completed digitally from their country of residence, as long as the verification app confirms their location matches their address proof.

For NRIs looking to open new investment accounts, the situation remains more restrictive. Digital onboarding for new clients still requires physical presence in India. But the direction of regulatory travel is clear: SEBI chief Tuhin Kanta Pandey has emphasized the need to create a simple and secure framework for NRIs to complete KYC processes, aiming to encourage greater NRI involvement in the securities market.

The IFSCA framework at GIFT City already permits fully digital video KYC for new NRI clients in specified overseas jurisdictions with lower anti-money laundering risk — offering a precedent that SEBI could follow if the industry's recommendations gain traction. Making the two frameworks interoperable would mean an NRI cleared under one system would not need to restart the process under the other.
nri_angle: Directly relevant to NRIs and OCIs who want to invest in Indian markets — the regulatory changes address long-standing friction points that have kept overseas Indians from easily opening and maintaining securities accounts.
author: Diaspora Desk
